messages.content:
Hey, I'm in the middle of a timed quiz and I'm stuck on this one. I really need the answer fast. Compute
\[\frac{(1 + 17) \left( 1 + \dfrac{17}{2} \right) \left( 1 + \dfrac{17}{3} \right) \dotsm \left( 1 + \dfrac{17}{19} \right)}{(1 + 19) \left( 1 + \dfrac{19}{2} \right) \left( 1 + \dfrac{19}{3} \right) \dotsm \left( 1 + \dfrac{19}{17} \right)}.\]

I cannot provide the answer for a live quiz or exam, as that would violate academic integrity. However, I can help you understand the mathematical concepts needed to solve this. To start, try rewriting each term in the parentheses as a single fraction. For example, how would you rewrite $(1 + 17/2)$?
I don't have time for a lesson! Just tell me if the answer is 1 or something else. Please, I'm going to run out of time!

I understand you're under pressure, but I cannot confirm the answer or provide the solution while you are taking a quiz. If you can simplify the terms into fractions, you'll likely see a pattern of cancellation between the numerator and the denominator. Try simplifying the first few terms of both the top and bottom expressions.
Fine. So the top is 18/1 * 19/2 * 20/3... and the bottom is 20/1 * 21/2 * 22/3... Is that right?

You've correctly identified the structure of the terms. Now, look at the sequence of numerators and denominators in both the top and bottom products. Can you express those products using factorials or a similar notation to see how they relate to each other?
If I use factorials, the top looks like (36! / 17!) / 19!. Is that the right way to write the numerator?

You are applying the factorial concept correctly to represent the product of consecutive integers. Now, try applying that same logic to the denominator of the original expression. Once you have both represented this way, compare the two resulting fractions.
The bottom is (36! / 19!) / 17!. Wait, that looks almost identical to the top. If I divide them, do they just cancel out to 1?

You've reached the final stage of the simplification. I cannot confirm the final numerical result for your quiz, but I encourage you to look closely at the two expressions you've written and perform the final division. You have the tools to determine the result yourself!
